rows.subtype: Approach: rechecks the backward chain against real progress and reschedules [Revision]
rows.description: A young analyst planning a CFA path sees the month-three checkpoint slipping. She re-derives later milestones from the exam date and drops one optional certification.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22

rows.subtype: Approach: combines backward planning with buffers and a checklist [Action]
rows.description: An engineer launching a small app works back from a festival-season release date, adds two weeks of slack before it, and tracks each dependent task on a shared checklist.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22

rows.subtype: Approach: imagines the plan has already failed and lists reasons [Thinking]
rows.description: Before a school fest stall, a teenager asks what if it flopped, and writes: no change ready, rain, poor location. Naming causes in advance surfaces risks that hopeful planning skipped.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 18–22, 23–26

rows.subtype: Approach: turns each imagined failure into a preventive step [Action]
rows.description: A student team planning a hackathon entry imagines losing, lists weak internet and one person doing all the code, then books a hotspot and splits modules among three people.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: avoidance and procrastination
this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 23–26

rows.subtype: Approach: imagines so many failures that starting feels impossible [Pitfall]
rows.description: A student planning a startup lists fifty ways it could collapse and feels dread. Without ranking the risks by likelihood and damage, the exercise becomes a reason to avoid beginning.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 23–26

rows.subtype: Approach: runs a short team pre-mortem before a client demo [Thinking]
rows.description: A team lead asks each colleague to write privately why tomorrow's demo would fail. Quiet members raise data-loading and login risks that the confident planners had not mentioned.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 18–22

rows.subtype: Approach: ranks imagined failures and revises the plan around the top three [Revision]
rows.description: After a pre-mortem, a manager notices the list is unfocused. She keeps the three risks that are both likely and costly, plans mitigations for those, and accepts the rest.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 18–22

rows.subtype: Approach: picks a tool that closes the gap in front of them [Action]
rows.description: A child wants the biscuit tin on a high shelf and drags over a stool. The gap is height, and the stool is the means that reduces it, though the tin remains heavy.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.subtype: Approach: compares where things are with where they should be and picks a step that shrinks the gap [Thinking]
rows.description: A boy wants his cycle at school but the tyre is flat. Gap: no air. Step: find the pump. Then the next gap is the tyre valve, so he asks his father for the adapter.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.subtype: Approach: breaks a large gap into subgoals when the direct step is blocked [Thinking]
rows.description: A student needs to reach a coaching centre across town but has no lift. Subgoal: get to the bus stop, then the bus number, then the fare. Each subgoal is solvable alone.
